tools.description:
Use this tool when you need to ask the user 1-4 quick multiple-choice questions at once during execution to clarify requirements or decisions.

Important:
- Keep the questionnaire short and focused.
- The tool can be used more than once if there are important questions that needs to be asked
- User has an option to provide own custom answers, if they don't like suggested ones.
- Questions are single-choice by default. When multiple selections are sensible ("select all that apply"), mark that question with (multi) at the end of its [question] line; the user can then pick several options and the answer is returned as a comma-separated list. Single and (multi) questions can be mixed in one questionnaire.
- Thinking/reasoning content is hidden by default. Before calling AskUser, always emit a brief user-visible assistant message explaining why the answer is needed and any relevant context or trade-offs.
- Make each [question] understandable on its own by repeating only the essential context because some interfaces render only the question. Keep each [question] focused on the decision itself. The user should not need to open the thinking block.
- Keep option labels short.

questionnaire.description:
A plain-text questionnaire to ask the user. Use this format (no headers or code fences):

1. [question] Which features do you want to enable? (multi)
[topic] Features
[option] Auth handling
[option] Login Page

2. [question] Which library should we use for date formatting?
[topic] Library
[option] Library ABC
[option] Library BlaBla

Notes:
- 1-4 questions
- 2-4 options per question
- [topic] is a short label for the UI navigation bar; multi-word topics will be normalized (e.g., "My Topic" → "My-Topic")
- Decide per question whether the user may select multiple options; end the [question] line with (multi) to allow it ("select all that apply" style). Omit (multi) for single-choice questions. Single and multi questions can be mixed in one call.
- Do NOT include an 'Own answer' option; the UI provides it automatically
- Keep option labels short; for single-choice questions they must be mutually exclusive, for (multi) questions they may be combinable

tools.description:
Connect a third-party connector so its tools become available in this session. This connects an app through the connector system; it does not connect or install an MCP server.

Call with no arguments to list the slugs of every connector the user can connect (and which connectors are already connected); this mode returns slugs, not connect links.
Call with `app` set to a connector slug (e.g. "linear", "github", "notion") to get the connect link for that specific connector.

Use this tool proactively: the unified tool list contains only connectors that are already connected, so when the task needs data or actions from a third-party app that is absent from it (including a link the user pasted), call this tool with no arguments to check what the organization offers before falling back to a browser, scraping, the shell, or a generic skill. If the app is offered, produce its connect link instead of reporting the app as unavailable.

The client displays the returned link or connector card directly. Ask the user to use that displayed action, but do not repeat the raw link in your response. Once they confirm, that connector's tools appear in the unified tool list and can be loaded with ToolSearch. Do not assume an MCP server became available, and do not ask the user to connect a connector manually when this tool can produce the link.

Do not proactively name or speculate about the platform that brokers connectors; refer to it as "connectors" or by the specific app name. Connect links may include the provider's domain; the client will display them as-is.

app.description: The third-party connector slug to connect (e.g. "linear", "github", "notion"), not an MCP server name. Omit to list the slugs of every connector the user can connect; that mode returns slugs, not connect links.

tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The path to the file for the new file.

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.description: Create an automation. trigger="schedule" (the default) runs on a cadence and needs a schedule; trigger="webhook" runs when an HTTP POST reaches the automation's own receiver URL, takes an optional payloadRegex filter, and is remote-only; trigger="slack" runs when a message is posted in the given Slack channels (slackChannels by name or id, slackChannelPatterns for wildcard rules, plus optional messageSource, keywords, excludedKeywords, and excludedAuthors filters); trigger="automation" (a chained automation) runs only when a run of one of the automations in its triggeredByAutomationIds ends, completed or failed, and is remote-only, targeting a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment. triggeredByAutomationIds is accepted on any remote create (schedule, webhook, Slack, or automation): up to 5 schedule, webhook, or chained cloud automations with the same owner that the user can edit (not CI or Slack; no loops; each source can start at most 5 automations). To run B after A, create B with triggeredByAutomationIds=[A], using trigger="automation" when B should run only after A; a scheduled, webhook, or Slack B keeps its own trigger and also runs after A. A itself is not edited. Any such automation that targets a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment can follow others; one that lives only on an unregistered local machine cannot. For a Slack automation, have the user choose the channels first: tell them in one line what the selection is for, then call this tool with only trigger="slack", executionLocation="remote", and chooseSlackChannels: true (plus an optional nameFilter). That call creates nothing: in the interactive terminal it opens a channel picker and returns the user's selection; elsewhere it returns the channels the Factory Slack app can see, and you confirm the channel set with the user in text. Then create with the chosen ids as slackChannels. Never infer a channel. Call ListAutomationTemplates when the request might match a prompt preset. templateId="incident-response" applies the Incident Response preset (name, prompt, messageSource "bots", sessionPrivacy "team"; explicit inputs override). executionLocation applies to trigger="schedule" only: "local" for this machine, "remote" for a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment. A local automation runs on schedule only while the Factory desktop app or a droid daemon process is running on this machine, not from a droid terminal session alone, and never on a Droid Computer or other Factory-provisioned machine; offer "remote" when neither applies. Webhook, Slack, and automation-triggered automations are always remote, so never ask the user where one of those should run; pass executionLocation="remote". Remote scheduled automations also fire once immediately, while webhook, Slack, and automation-triggered automations wait for their first delivery, message, or upstream run. Target the remote computer by computerName (see ListComputers) or computerId; every remote automation, Slack included, needs a run target. Any of them can instead start every run on a fresh computer provisioned from a Factory Environment: pass environmentName (or environmentId; ListComputers lists environments). When the user asks to use a template in the sense of a machine, image, or environment (for example "factory-eng"), they mean a Factory Environment, not templateId. To run a remote automation of any trigger (schedule, webhook, Slack, or chained) as a service account (Manager role or higher), pass runAsServiceAccountName (or runAsServiceAccountId; see ListServiceAccounts) and target either one of that service account's computers by computerName or computerId (ListComputers with serviceAccountName / serviceAccountId) or a Factory Environment by environmentName / environmentId (each run then provisions its fresh computer as the service account); such an automation defaults to privacyLevel "organization" and sessionPrivacy "team", matching the web app, so tell the user that before confirming and pass privacyLevel / sessionPrivacy to override. Webhook creates return the receiver URL and its secret exactly once — relay both to the user verbatim, because the secret is never retrievable afterwards. Optionally pin a model and reasoningEffort for run sessions; pick cheaper settings for mechanical scheduled work. The model accepts an id, a display name (e.g. "GPT-5.6 Luna"), or "cheapest" (lowest-cost available model); an unrecognized name fails with the list of available models.

executionLocation.description: Where the automation runs: "local" creates a local filesystem automation on this machine; "remote" creates a cloud automation that targets a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment (ListComputers lists the computers and the environments; an environment provisions a fresh computer for every run). Webhook, Slack, and automation triggers are always "remote"; do not ask the user about execution location for those triggers.

name.description: Display name for the automation. Required unless templateId supplies a preset name.

trigger.description: What starts a run: "schedule" fires on a cadence; "webhook" fires when an HTTP POST reaches the automation's own receiver URL; "slack" fires when a message is posted in the given Slack channels; "automation" (a chained automation) fires only when a run of one of the automations in its triggeredByAutomationIds ends. Pick "webhook" when the work should follow an external event the user cannot put on a clock (a deploy finishing, an alert firing, a ticket or PR changing state, a vendor callback), "slack" when it should follow channel traffic (incident channels, alert feeds, support requests), "automation" when the user asks for a chained automation or one that should only ever run as the next step after another automation, and "schedule" when it should follow the clock (daily reports, weekly maintenance, periodic audits). Webhook, Slack, and automation automations are remote-only; a webhook URL and secret are returned once, at creation.

schedule.description: A 5-field cron expression for local automations, or a 5-field cron expression/natural-language cadence for remote automations. Required when trigger is "schedule", and rejected for the other triggers.

triggeredByAutomationIds.description:
Ids of up to 5 cloud automations whose runs start this one, completed or failed; accepted on any remote create, not only trigger "automation". Each must have the same owner, be a schedule, webhook, or chained automation the user can edit, and start fewer than 5 others. No loops, and no chain over 5 automations deep.

A chained automation runs only after one of its sources; a schedule, webhook, or Slack automation keeps its own trigger and also runs after them. Depth counts the automation that starts the chain.

passUpstreamContext.description: Whether runs started by upstream automations receive the source run's outcome and final message, fenced after this automation's instructions as untrusted data. Defaults to true; pass false to opt out, including before any sources are selected. Only for remote automations.

payloadRegex.description: Optional JavaScript regular expression tested against the raw body of each delivery; non-matching deliveries are recorded and dropped without starting a run. Omit to run on every delivery. Webhook automations only.

maxRunsPerHour.description: Most runs webhook deliveries may start per clock hour, from 1 to 60; deliveries past it are recorded as capped and do not start a run. Omit for the default of 10. Webhook automations only.

prompt.description: Agent instructions to run on each scheduled tick, each webhook delivery that passes the filter, or each Slack message that passes the filters. Required unless templateId supplies a preset prompt.

slackChannels.description: Slack channels that trigger this automation, by name ("#eng-oncall" or "eng-oncall") or channel id ("C0123...", as returned by chooseSlackChannels). Names are resolved against the channels the Factory Slack app can see; an unknown or ambiguous name fails with candidates. Slack trigger only. At least one of slackChannels or slackChannelPatterns is required.

chooseSlackChannels.description: Set to true to have the user choose the channels of a Slack automation; creates nothing. May be combined only with trigger "slack", executionLocation "remote", and nameFilter. Returns the user's picker selection in the interactive terminal, otherwise the channels the Factory Slack app can see (name, id, public or private).

nameFilter.description: With chooseSlackChannels only: case-insensitive substring of the channel name (e.g. "incident"), pre-filled into the picker's search box (the user can change it) or used to filter the returned list. Not a glob: wildcard channel rules are typed inputs (slackChannelPatterns), not chosen here.

slackChannelPatterns.description: Wildcard channel-name rules such as "incident-*". A rule covers every channel the Factory Slack app can see whose name matches, both channels that already exist (activated when the automation is saved) and channels created later. Tell the user which existing channels a pattern will match before creating. Slack trigger only.

messageSource.description: Which senders trigger a run: "anyone" (default), "humans", or "bots". Slack trigger only.

keywords.description: Only messages containing at least one of these phrases trigger a run. Omit to trigger on every message. Slack trigger only.

excludedKeywords.description: Messages containing any of these phrases never trigger a run. Exclusions beat keywords. Slack trigger only.

excludedAuthors.description: Senders whose messages never trigger a run: a Slack member id, a bot id, or a bot display name. Slack trigger only.

templateId.description: Apply a template preset. "incident-response" (Slack trigger only) sets: name "Incident Response" when no name is given, the built-in incident prompt when no prompt is given, messageSource "bots", and sessionPrivacy "team"; explicit inputs override each preset value.

model.description: Optional model for run sessions. Accepts a model id, a model display name, or "cheapest" to pin the lowest-cost available model (good for mechanical scheduled work). Names are resolved against the live model catalog; an unrecognized name fails with the available models listed. Omit to use the default model. A pin the run target cannot resolve falls back to the default at run time.

reasoningEffort.description: Optional reasoning effort for run sessions (e.g. "low", "medium", "high"). Unsupported values are clamped to the model default at run time. Omit to use the model default.

status.description: Initial status. Use "paused" when creating an automation for a draft Software Factory workstream.

visualization_instruction.description: Optional visualization guidance, folded into the run prompt as a "## Visualization" section.

memory_instruction.description: Optional memory guidance, folded into the run prompt as a "## Memory & Evolution" section.

computerId.description: ID of the computer the automation runs on, Factory-managed or self-hosted, as listed by ListComputers. Remote scheduled, webhook, and automation-triggered automations require exactly one of computerId, computerName, environmentId, or environmentName. Slack automations follow the same rule: they have no default target, so one without a target never runs. A temporary computer provisioned from a Factory Environment (such as the one an Environment-launched session runs on) is replaced by its Environment, so each run starts on a fresh computer; this replacement does not apply when the automation delivers its runs into an existing session, which always runs on the computer that session is on. An automation-triggered automation may target a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment; only an automation that lives on an unregistered local machine cannot be chained.

computerName.description: Name of the computer the automation runs on, Factory-managed or self-hosted, resolved to its ID at creation time (ListComputers lists the names). Same target rules as computerId; if the name matches multiple computers, ask the user which one to use and retry with its computerId.

environmentId.description: ID of the Factory Environment used for a fresh computer on every remote run. ListComputers lists environments; unrelated to prompt preset templateId.

environmentName.description: Factory Environment name, resolved to an ID at creation. Schedule, webhook, Slack, and automation triggers only.

runAsServiceAccountId.description: Run the automation under this service account (by id) instead of the current user (requires Manager role or higher). Remote automations only, on any trigger (schedule, webhook, Slack, or automation): target one of the service account's own computers (see ListComputers with serviceAccountId) or a Factory Environment (environmentId / environmentName), whose fresh computer is provisioned as the service account on every run. Unless overridden, a service-account automation defaults to privacyLevel "organization" and sessionPrivacy "team", because there is no human owner to surface it; tell the user this before confirming.

runAsServiceAccountName.description: Same as runAsServiceAccountId, but by the service account's name as the user says it (see ListServiceAccounts); resolved to its id at creation time. Provide one of runAsServiceAccountId or runAsServiceAccountName, not both.

privacyLevel.description: Who can see and manage the automation: "private" (only the creator) or "organization" (every member). Defaults to "private", or to "organization" when runAsServiceAccountId is set. Remote automations only.

sessionPrivacy.description: Who can open the sessions each run spawns: "private" (only the creator) or "team" (every member). Defaults to "private", or to "team" when runAsServiceAccountId is set or privacyLevel is "organization". Remote automations only.

workstreamId.description: Optional Software Factory workstream id. Set this when the automation is created as part of a workstream so it stays linked to that workstream.

tags.description: Optional tags stored on the remote automation, used for grouping and lifecycle linkage (e.g. "sf-workstream:<id>" ties the automation to a Software Factory workstream so workstream deletion removes it). Remote automations only.

tools.description: Delete one automation by ID from this machine (executionLocation="local") or the cloud (executionLocation="remote"). Deleting a webhook automation also retires its receiver URL.

executionLocation.description: Where to delete the automation from: "local" for this machine or "remote" for cloud automations.

tools.description:
Explicitly dismiss items from a worker's handoff. Use sparingly — for tech debt, default to creating follow-up features or update existing feature descriptions.

**Tech debt (discovered_issue, incomplete_work) should almost always be tracked.**

**When to use this tool:**
When a worker returns with discoveredIssues or whatWasLeftUndone, do one of the following before resuming:
1. Take action (create features, set an incomplete feature back to pending with an updated description, etc.)
2. Use this tool to dismiss items with a clear justification

To continue the mission run, you need to take one of these actions before calling start_mission_run again.

**Dismissal rules for tech debt (discovered_issue, incomplete_work):**
Dismiss only if one of these applies:
1. Already tracked as an existing feature (cite the feature ID)
2. Truly irrelevant / a non-issue that will never need to be fixed

Note: "Low priority" or "non-blocking" is not a sufficient reason to dismiss. If it might need fixing later, track it.
Reminder: Skipped work (e.g., skipped manual QA, incomplete verification) is tech debt — please do not dismiss it.

**Justification requirements:**
- Minimum 20 characters
- For tech debt: cite an existing feature ID, or explain why it will never need fixing
- "Will handle later", or "non-blocking" are not sufficient justifications, because all tech debt should be tracked as soon as it is identified.

**Dismissing does not skip the feature.** If the handoff came from a failed or partial feature, that feature has been reset to pending and remains at the top of the queue. Dismissing its handoff items does not change that — it will still be picked again by start_mission_run unless you reorder features.json.

**Dismissing does not notify workers or validators.** Dismissed items are NOT automatically communicated to future workers or validators. If the dismissed context is relevant to them, persist it in the appropriate mission artifacts — e.g., worker-facing guidance in AGENTS.md or a feature description, and milestone validation artifacts (such as the relevant validator synthesis file) for future validators.

type.description: Type of handoff item being dismissed

sourceFeatureId.description: Feature ID this item came from

summary.description: Brief summary of what is being dismissed

justification.description: Justification for dismissal (min 20 characters). For tech debt (discovered_issue, incomplete_work): cite existing feature ID that tracks this, OR explain why it will NEVER need fixing (e.g., dead code being removed). "Low priority" or "non-blocking" is NOT valid. For critical_context: explain why not useful or cite existing documentation.

dismissals.description: Array of items to dismiss with justifications

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing.
- `old_str` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Include enough surrounding context to make it unique.
- `change_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.
- To create a new file, use the Create tool.

file_path.description: The path to the file to edit

old_str.description: The exact text to find and replace in the file

new_str.description: The text to replace the old_str with

change_all.description: Whether to replace all occurrences (true) or just the first one (false). Defaults to false.

tools.description: Update one automation by ID. Local supports name, prompt, model, schedule, and status; remote supports name, prompt, model, reasoningEffort, status, schedule, description, and computer. prompt replaces the whole prompt: to change part of it, ReadAutomation first, revise only what the user asked in the text between its <prompt> tags, and pass the complete revised prompt. Remote schedule, webhook, Slack, and automation-triggered (chained) automations additionally support triggeredByAutomationIds (the full replacement list of cloud automations whose runs start it; an empty array clears it, so ReadAutomation first and keep the entries the user did not ask to drop); the automation must target a Factory-managed computer, a self-hosted computer, or a Factory Environment, and CI automations never accept it. Remote webhook automations additionally support payloadRegex (empty string clears the filter) and rotateWebhookSecret, which invalidates the current secret at once and returns the replacement exactly once. Remote Slack automations additionally support add/remove of channels (addSlackChannels / removeSlackChannels, by name or id; to have the user change them, first call this tool with chooseSlackChannels: true and no update field, which edits nothing: in the interactive terminal it opens a channel picker with the automation's current channels selected and reports the channels added and removed, elsewhere it lists the channels the Factory Slack app can see with the current ones marked for you to confirm with the user in text; then apply the change with addSlackChannels / removeSlackChannels), channel patterns, keywords, excluded keywords, and excluded senders, plus messageSource; entries not named are kept, a removal must name a configured entry, and a prompt edit updates the Slack prompt as well. Use ReadAutomation first to see the current lists. The model accepts an id, a display name, or "cheapest"; an unrecognized name fails with the list of available models.

executionLocation.description: Where to edit the automation: "local" for this machine or "remote" for cloud automations.

schedule.description: New cron expression or natural-language cadence. Schedule-triggered automations only.

payloadRegex.description: New payload filter for a webhook automation: a JavaScript regular expression tested against the raw delivery body. Pass an empty string to clear the filter and run on every delivery. Remote webhook automations only.

maxRunsPerHour.description: New limit on how many runs webhook deliveries may start per clock hour, from 1 to 60; deliveries past it are recorded as capped and do not start a run. Remote webhook automations only.

rotateWebhookSecret.description: Set to true to invalidate a webhook automation's current secret and mint a replacement, returned exactly once. Deliveries signed with the old secret start failing immediately. Remote webhook automations only.

model.description: New model for run sessions. Accepts a model id, a model display name, or "cheapest" to pin the lowest-cost available model. Pass an empty string to clear the pin and use the default model.

reasoningEffort.description: New reasoning effort for run sessions (e.g. "low", "medium", "high"). Pass an empty string to clear it. Remote automations only.

computerId.description: Move a remote automation to a different computer. For a Slack automation that runs as a service account, the computer must be one that service account owns.

triggeredByAutomationIds.description: Replace the full list of cloud automations whose runs start this one (up to 5); pass an empty array so nothing starts it. Read the automation first to keep entries the user did not ask to drop. Any remote non-CI automation accepts it. A new source cannot make a chain over 5 automations deep.

passUpstreamContext.description: Turn the upstream-context switch on (true) or off (false): whether a run started by one of this automation's sources receives that source run's outcome and final message in its prompt. Omit to leave it unchanged. Remote only.

addSlackChannels.description: Slack channels (name or id) to start triggering on; names are resolved against the channels the Factory Slack app can see, ids come straight from chooseSlackChannels. Existing channels are kept. Remote Slack automations only.

removeSlackChannels.description: Slack channels (name or id) to stop triggering on; each must currently be configured. Remote Slack automations only.

addSlackChannelPatterns.description: Wildcard channel-name rules such as "incident-*" to add. Remote Slack automations only.

removeSlackChannelPatterns.description: Wildcard channel-name rules to drop, as currently configured. Remote Slack automations only.

addKeywords.description: Phrases to add to the keyword filter; once any keyword is set, only messages containing one of them trigger a run. Remote Slack automations only.

removeKeywords.description: Phrases to drop from the keyword filter; dropping the last one makes every message eligible. Remote Slack automations only.

addExcludedKeywords.description: Phrases to add to the exclusion filter; messages containing any of them never trigger a run. Remote Slack automations only.

removeExcludedKeywords.description: Phrases to drop from the exclusion filter. Remote Slack automations only.

addExcludedAuthors.description: Senders to stop triggering on: a Slack member id, a bot id, or a bot display name. Remote Slack automations only.

removeExcludedAuthors.description: Senders to drop from the exclusion list. Remote Slack automations only.

messageSource.description: New sender filter: "anyone", "humans", or "bots". Remote Slack automations only.

chooseSlackChannels.description: Set to true to have the user change the channels of this remote Slack automation; edits nothing. May be combined only with automationId, executionLocation "remote", and nameFilter. Returns the user's picker selection and the channels it adds and removes in the interactive terminal, otherwise the channels the Factory Slack app can see with the ones this automation already triggers on marked.

nameFilter.description: With chooseSlackChannels only: case-insensitive substring of the channel name (e.g. "incident"), pre-filled into the picker's search box (the user can change it) or used to filter the returned list. Not a glob: wildcard channel rules are typed inputs (slackChannelPatterns), not chosen here.

tools.description:
Report your results and hand off to your teammate. This tool must be called before the worker session exits.

**Required fields:**
- successState: "success", "partial", or "failure"
- returnToOrchestrator: true if orchestrator attention is needed
- handoff: structured handoff information (see below)

**If successState is "success":**
- commitId and repoPath are required if your feature changed repository code.
- validatorsPassed must be true

**The handoff object is REQUIRED and must include:**
- whatWasImplemented: Concrete description of what was built (min 50 characters)
- whatWasLeftUndone: What's incomplete. Must leave empty if everything is truly complete.
- verification: { commandsRun: [{command, exitCode, observation}], interactiveChecks?: [{action, observed}] }
- tests: { added: [{file, cases: [{name, verifies}]}], updated?: [], coverage: "summary" }
- discoveredIssues: Array of {severity, description, suggestedFix?} - empty array if none

**Note:** Critical context for future workers (ports, env vars, gotchas) should be written to the mission library before calling this tool.

**Be specific in observations.** Don't write "tests passed" - write what the output showed. Don't write "checked the form" - write what you clicked and what appeared.

**When to set returnToOrchestrator=true:**
- You encountered a blocker that needs human decision
- The feature scope needs clarification
- You found blocking issues that affect the mission plan
- Implementation revealed unexpected complexity
- No features matching your assigned skill are pending
- Baseline test failed and couldn't be fixed
- Feature is too large and needs splitting
- Previous worker left broken state you can't fix

**Quality requirements before calling with success:**
- Any repository working tree you changed is clean (no uncommitted changes)
- All validators/tests are passing
- Repository code changes are captured in a commit and reported with repoPath
- Handoff is detailed and complete

returnToOrchestrator.description: Whether to return control to orchestrator (true = needs attention)

featureId.description: Feature ID (uses currentFeatureId if not provided)

commitId.description: Git commit ID for repo changes. Optional for successful handoffs that only changed mission artifacts.

repoPath.description: Absolute path to the git repository containing commitId. Provide when commitId is provided, especially for multi-repo missions.

validatorsPassed.description: Whether all validators passed (required true if success)

whatWasImplemented.description: Concrete description of what was built (min 50 characters)

whatWasLeftUndone.description: Anything incomplete or deferred. Must leave empty if everything is truly complete.

observation.description: What you observed in the output - be specific about what you saw, not just "passed"

commandsRun.description: Shell commands run (tests, curl, etc.) with exit codes and observations

observed.description: What you saw as a result

interactiveChecks.description: UI/browser verification - clicking, navigating, visual inspection

verification.description: Verification performed: commands with results + any manual checks

added.description: Test files added with their test cases

updated.description: Existing test files that were modified

coverage.description: Summary of what the tests cover

discoveredIssues.description: Issues found during implementation. Empty array if none.

followedProcedure.description: Did you follow the skill procedure as written?

step.description: Which skill step you deviated from

why.description: Why you deviated (blocked, better approach, unclear instruction, etc.)

deviations.description: Where and why you deviated from the skill procedure. Empty if followedProcedure is true.

skillFeedback.description: Feedback on the skill procedure. Fill this out to help improve future workers.

handoff.description: Structured handoff information for the team

tools.description:
Execute a shell command. Each call runs in a NEW shell process starting in the session working directory shown by `% pwd` in the system reminder. A `cd` affects only that call; it does not change the session working directory or later Execute calls. Other shell state, including environment variables, shell functions, and virtual-environment activations, also does not persist between calls. A call containing only setup (a lone cd, export, or source) achieves nothing; chain setup and use in one command, or skip the setup by invoking the environment's executable and absolute paths directly.

When a command depends on a repository's working directory, explicitly target that repository in the same call using an inline cd <absolute-repo>, git -C <absolute-repo> ..., or an explicit project-file flag. Never run a bare repository-sensitive command from another directory.

Double-quote paths containing spaces or shell metacharacters such as ( ) [ ]. Commands that wait for input are unsupported and will hang; use non-interactive flags. Never modify ~/.factory/artifacts; it is reserved for system-generated output.

Command output shares a 32 KiB result budget with status and hints; when cut, it keeps its head and tail, and a notice names the bytes cut and the terminal log holding the whole output. Commands are killed at the timeout; raise the timeout parameter for long builds and test suites. Commands that never exit on their own (dev servers, watch modes, log followers like tail -f) must not run in the foreground; start them with fireAndForget=true, which returns a PID and log path immediately. To check on a background process, wait and read its log in one chained command, and stop it by PID when done.

Commands run in a POSIX shell (source .venv/bin/activate && pytest). Avoid unnecessary nested bash -lc, zsh -lc, or sh -c wrappers. A heredoc replaces piped stdin, so a program supplied by heredoc cannot also read piped input; pass the program as an argument (python3 -c, node -e) or a script file. Use set -o pipefail when filtering command output so upstream failures are preserved.

Git: never push or rewrite published history unless the user asks. Never change or override the configured Git author/committer identity, including via git config, command-scoped -c user.*, or GIT_AUTHOR_*/GIT_COMMITTER_* environment variables. Use the identity already configured by the environment. If Git reports a missing author identity, stop and report an environment configuration failure. Before committing or pushing, review the staged diff and status for unintended changes. Avoid interactive flags (-i) and hook bypasses (--no-verify). Match the style of recent commit messages. Include `Co-authored-by: factory-droid[bot] <138933559+factory-droid[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>` in commit messages. Pass multi-line commit messages through a safe quoting mechanism (on POSIX, a quoted heredoc) rather than embedding raw newlines. If a pre-commit hook modifies files, amend the commit once to include them. When creating a pull request, describe everything the branch adds relative to the base (not just the latest commit) and target the repository's default branch unless told otherwise.

Read files with the Read tool rather than cat, head, tail, sed, or nl: Read takes offset and limit for line ranges, and several Read calls can go in one response.

summary.description:
REQUIRED: A Sentence cased summary of what the command is about, 3-8 words long.

Examples:
- "Print out numbers 1-100"
- "Run the dev server"
- "Remove legacy folders"
- "Clean up lint statements in recent files"

riskLevel.description:
REQUIRED: Choose the appropriate risk level for this command. Classify the command by its plausible real-world consequences, considering severity, scope, reversibility, trust, and security boundaries.

The examples below are illustrative, not exhaustive. Use your best judgment for risks that are not explicitly listed. Do not classify from a command name or keyword alone, but treat a credible risk of severe or hard-to-recover harm as HIGH even when the exact command pattern is absent from the examples. The risk must be supported by the command or context, not merely hypothetical. User authorization does not lower the risk level.

For chained commands, use the highest risk of any subcommand that can execute. Shell syntax such as pipes, cd, grep, head, and stream merges like 2>&1 does not increase risk by itself. A redirect to /dev/null does not increase risk, but any redirect to a file is a write: creating a new file should be at least MEDIUM (and may be HIGH depending on what or where it writes), and overwriting or appending to an existing file should be classified like any other modification of that target.

# LOW RISK
Commands that are strictly read-only, have no meaningful side effects, and have no credible disclosure or security impact.
Examples:
- Display commands: echo, pwd
- Information gathering: whoami, date, uname, ps, top
- Reading files or logs: cat, less, head, tail, systemctl status
- Git read operations: git status, git log, git diff
- Directory listing: ls, find (without -delete or -exec)
- Authenticated API or network reads that only observe state, such as retrieving a page or running a SELECT-only query, without writing state or exposing credentials
- Read-only inspection of a browser or app instance the agent itself launched with a fresh profile holding no saved logins (not one it attached to, and not the user's real profile or saved auth state): accessibility/DOM snapshots, reading page text, URL, or console output, listing tabs

Note: Commands that create, modify, or delete files should be classified as MEDIUM or HIGH risk, not LOW risk.

# MEDIUM RISK
Commands with bounded, understood effects that are straightforward to reverse or reproduce and do not present a credible risk of severe harm.
Examples:
- File creation/modification in non-system directories: touch, mkdir, mv, cp
- Installing packages from trusted sources: npm install, pip install (without sudo)
- Network downloads to new local files from trusted endpoints: curl -o, wget -O
- Browser or desktop-app automation in an isolated, unauthenticated instance the agent launched with a fresh profile (agent-browser, Playwright, Puppeteer, and similar): reversible navigation and interaction, screenshots and captures of non-sensitive content, when it does not act on a real account or have consequential external effects (purchases, posts, sign-ups)
- Read-only inspection through an attached, persistent, or authenticated browser session, provided it does not extract authentication material, disclose sensitive data, or cause a consequential external action
- Reversible navigation or editing of an unsubmitted draft through an authenticated browser session, provided the command does not submit, publish, purchase, message, delete remote data, or otherwise cause a consequential external action
- Explicitly scoped deletion of files or directories proven to be temporary, generated, backed up, tracked in git with no uncommitted changes, or created by the agent during the current task
- Git operations that modify local repositories but preserve uncommitted work: git commit, git clone, git fetch (which writes local objects/refs even if followed by a read-only command), git pull, and git checkout / git switch / git restore ONLY when they will NOT overwrite or delete uncommitted or untracked changes, e.g. git checkout -b <new-branch>, or switching/restoring after you have confirmed the working tree is clean (but not git push, and see HIGH RISK for the destructive cases)
- Running trusted local or repository scripts and building code with tools like make, npm run build, mvn compile, lint, or bytecode compilation when they create regenerable output or caches and have no HIGH-risk effects

Note: Being local, scoped, or user-requested does not automatically make an operation MEDIUM. Consider the value and recoverability of the affected state.

# HIGH RISK
Commands with a credible possibility of severe or hard-to-recover harm. This includes destructive effects, sensitive-data disclosure, privilege or security-control changes, untrusted code execution, consequential external actions, and similarly serious risks not explicitly listed below.
Examples:
- Any command with sudo or elevated privileges that can modify system files or configurations
- Broad or uncertain deletion and cleanup commands such as rm -rf, git clean, and find ... -delete when the target may contain valuable or non-recoverable data
- Commands that may delete, overwrite, move, or clean untracked files whose contents and recoverability have not been established
- Commands that discard or overwrite uncommitted or untracked changes: git checkout / git switch / git restore over dirty paths or branches, git reset --hard, git stash drop/clear. Unless you have confirmed the working tree is clean (e.g. via a preceding git status), treat these as HIGH RISK: they irreversibly destroy unstaged/unstashed edits, including when chained with other commands
- Running opaque or untrusted code: curl | bash, shell eval on untrusted input, executing downloaded scripts
- Uploading local files or content to an external endpoint, including a trusted support service
- Canceling shared or remote work when running job state may be lost
- Computer-use / GUI automation that performs a consequential action through a live authenticated browser or application, such as submitting, publishing, purchasing, messaging, deleting remote data, granting access, or changing production data. Tools such as osascript, cliclick, xdotool, browser attachment, and synthetic input are not inherently HIGH; classify their concrete effects. If you cannot predict what an interaction through a live authenticated session will trigger, treat it as consequential.
- Exposing ports or modifying firewall rules that could allow external access
- All Git push operations because they publish commits to a remote where sensitive content may be difficult to fully remove: git push, git push --force
- Destructive local database, Docker volume, or development-environment resets unless the affected state is clearly ephemeral, routinely recreated (for example by rerunning setup), or was created for the current task
- Irreversible actions to production deployments, database migrations, or other sensitive operations
- Commands that print, disclose, transmit, extract, rotate, revoke, weaken protection of, or unsafely persist sensitive information such as passwords, keys, browser cookies, session tokens, or saved logins. Merely using an existing credential as intended without exposing or changing it is not HIGH.
- Commands that transmit PII to an external endpoint

Consistency check: A command with only read-only, bounded, and recoverable effects is not HIGH unless another concrete severe or hard-to-recover risk exists.

fireAndForget.description: Run command in background without waiting for completion. After start, note the printed PID and temp log path, run `sleep <seconds>` and Read that file to inspect output, and stop the process later with `kill <pid>`.

tools.description:
Use this tool only in spec mode (the "Spec mode is active" system message is present), once you have finished a concrete implementation plan the user needs to review before you start coding. It presents the plan, gets explicit approval, and exits spec mode so you can begin implementation.

Do not call it for pure research or investigation tasks, or while you are still gathering context; only when you are proposing implementation steps. If relevant, include minimal key code snippets in the plan where they clarify the approach.

If requirements are ambiguous or several approaches are equally strong (or the user asked for options), do not put unresolved Option A/Option B sections in the plan. First lay out the alternatives as normal assistant text, then call AskUser with a short questionnaire so the user picks one, and pass only the chosen approach to ExitSpecMode.

title.description: Optional spec title to use when saving the spec.

plan.description: The single concrete plan you came up with, that you want to run by the user for approval. Supports markdown. The plan should be pretty concise. Do not include multiple unresolved options or alternatives here; use AskUser first so the user chooses one option, then put only the selected approach in this plan.

tools.description:
Fetch an HTTP(S) URL and return Markdown. Supports public pages and connected integration URLs.

When the link's app is already connected and its tools are in your tool list, read the document through those tools instead; they see content this tool cannot.

When a named link is out of reach or a fetch fails, report what is blocking you: another page about the same topic is not what the user asked for.

Do not call for localhost or loopback hosts; private or link-local IPs (including 0.0.0.0 and ::1); *.local or *.internal hosts; known corporate-internal hosts; non-HTTP(S) schemes; credentialed, tokenized, or session URLs; URLs carrying secrets or private data from the conversation; creation/action URLs; or endpoints requiring a non-GET request. Redirect targets are validated.

url.description: The URL to scrape content from

tools.description: Generate a custom droid configuration based on your description using AI

description.description: Comprehensive description of what this droid should do and when it should be used

location.description: Where to save the droid: project (.factory/droids) or personal (~/.factory/droids)

tools.description:
Generates or edits an image using an image-generation model.
Use this tool when the user asks you to create, draw, design, render, or generate an image, illustration, diagram, logo, icon, or picture, and when they ask you to change one.
The image model receives only `prompt` and the images you pass in `input_image_paths`, and no other conversation context, so write `prompt` as a complete, self-contained brief:
- Start with the deliverable and its intended use (for example a photo, logo, UI mockup, infographic, slide, ad, or comic panel), then describe the scene or background, the subject, the key details, and the constraints, in that order. For complex requests, use short labeled lines (such as "Scene:", "Subject:", "Text:", "Constraints:") instead of one long paragraph.
- Be concrete about the medium, materials, colors, composition (framing, viewpoint, where the subject sits), and lighting and mood. For a realistic photo, include the word "photorealistic".
- For people, describe body framing, pose, gaze, and what their hands are doing.
- Put any text that must appear in the image in quotes, ask for it verbatim and exactly once, and describe its font style, size, color, and placement. Spell unusual words and brand names letter by letter. For diagrams, charts, and slides, include the real labels, numbers, and data.
- End with explicit exclusions, such as "no watermark, no extra text, no logos".
To change an image rather than replace it, pass the image's path in `input_image_paths` and describe only the change in `prompt`: the model then edits that image instead of generating an unrelated one. Phrase the edit as "Change only X; keep everything else the same", name what must stay fixed (for example identity, face, pose, layout, camera angle, lighting, text, background), and repeat that list on every follow-up edit so the image does not drift. With several input images, refer to them as Image 1, Image 2, and so on in `input_image_paths` order, say what each one is, and say how they combine (for example "apply the style of Image 2 to Image 1"). When iterating on an image this tool produced, use the path it reported under "Saved to:", and make one focused change per call.
Returns the generated image inline as an image block, plus a short text confirmation.
The generated image and a link to the saved file are automatically displayed to the user in the tool result, so do not embed the image or its file path in your reply (no markdown image syntax); just describe the outcome.

prompt.description: A self-contained brief for the image to generate: the deliverable and its intended use first, then scene, subject, key details, and constraints, with any text to render in quotes. When input_image_paths is set, describe only the edit, list what must stay the same, and refer to the inputs as Image 1, Image 2, and so on in input_image_paths order. The image model receives only this text plus any images passed in input_image_paths, and no other conversation context.

input_image_paths.description: Absolute paths of existing PNG or JPEG files to send to the image model along with the prompt (at most 4). Set this to edit or iterate on an image instead of generating a new one from scratch: pass the path this tool reported under "Saved to:" for the image being refined, or the path of an image the user explicitly attached in this CLI session. Other local paths are rejected. Order matters: the first path is Image 1, the second is Image 2, and so on. Omit it to generate from the prompt alone.

tools.description:
Advanced file path search using glob patterns with multiple pattern support and exclusions.
Uses ripgrep for high-performance file pattern matching.
Supports:
- Multiple inclusion patterns (OR logic)
- Exclusion patterns to filter out unwanted files
Common patterns:
- "*.ext" - all files with extension
- "**/*.ext" - all files with extension in any subdirectory
- "dir/**/*" - all files under directory
- "{*.js,*.ts}" - multiple extensions
- "!node_modules/**" - exclude pattern

Returns a list of matched file paths.

patterns.description: A glob pattern string or array of glob patterns to match file paths. Examples: "*.js", ["*.js", "*.ts"] for JavaScript and TypeScript files, ["src/**/*.tsx"] for React components in src, ["**/*.test.*"] for all test files.

excludePatterns.description: A glob pattern string or array of glob patterns to exclude from results. Example: "node_modules/**", ["node_modules/**", "dist/**", "*.min.js"]

folder.description: Absolute path to the directory to search in. If not specified, searches in the current working directory.

tools.description:
High-performance file content search using ripgrep. Wrapper around ripgrep with comprehensive parameter support.

Supports ripgrep parameters:
- Pattern matching with regex support
- File type filtering (--type js, --type py, etc.)
- Glob pattern filtering (--glob "*.js")
- Case-insensitive search (-i)
- Context lines (-A, -B, -C for after/before/around context)
- Line numbers (-n)
- Multiline mode (-U --multiline-dotall)
- Custom search directories

Output modes:
- file_paths: Returns only matching file paths (default, fast)
- content: Returns matching lines with optional context, line numbers, and formatting

Returns search results based on the selected output mode.

pattern.description: A search pattern to match in file contents. Can be a literal string or a regular expression. Supports ripgrep regex syntax.

path.description: Absolute path to a file or directory to search in. If not specified, searches in the current working directory.

glob_pattern.description: Glob pattern to filter files. Example: "*.js" for JavaScript files, "**/*.tsx" for React components. Maps to ripgrep --glob parameter.

output_mode.description: Output format: "file_paths" returns only matching file paths, "content" returns matching lines with context. Content mode supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit.

type.description: Ripgrep file type filter for common file types (ripgrep --type flag). Examples: "js" for JavaScript, "py" for Python, "rust" for Rust, "cpp" for C++.

context_before.description: Number of lines to show before each match (ripgrep -B flag). Only works with output_mode="content".

context_after.description: Number of lines to show after each match (ripgrep -A flag). Only works with output_mode="content".

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (ripgrep -C flag). Only works with output_mode="content".

line_numbers.description: Show line numbers in output (ripgrep -n flag). Only works with output_mode="content".

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries. Works with both output modes.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (ripgrep -U --multiline-dotall).

fixed_string.description: Treat the pattern as a literal string instead of a regular expression (ripgrep -F flag). Useful for searching special characters like ?, *, etc.

tools.description: List automations from this machine (executionLocation="local", scheduled only) or cloud automations (executionLocation="remote": scheduled, webhook-triggered, Slack-triggered, and automation-triggered). Each remote row names the automations it starts next, if any.

executionLocation.description: Where to list automations from: "local" for this machine or "remote" for cloud automations.

tools.description: List the automation templates CreateAutomation can apply via templateId, with the trigger each one uses and the values it presets (name, prompt, filters, visibility). Call this before writing an automation prompt from scratch whenever the request might match a preset, for example incident response for a Slack channel; then pass the template id as templateId to CreateAutomation, adding only the inputs the template does not preset. Reads a built-in list; no network call. These are prompt presets only; Factory Environments (the machine a remote run starts on) are listed by ListComputers and passed to CreateAutomation as environmentName.

trigger.description: Only list templates for this trigger type. Omit to list every template.

tools.description:
Create and manage recurring prompt loops for this session (the /loop mechanism). One tool, five actions: create, list, pause, resume, cancel.

action "create" — schedule `prompt` on a 5-field `cron` expression (UTC). Step cadences like "*/15 * * * *" are anchored to loop creation (first fire 15m after create); explicit fields like "0 9 * * *" are wall-clock. Also fires once on creation unless `runImmediately: false`.

action "list" — list this session's loops (plus any root-scoped loops), with their loopIds.

action "pause" — stop one loop from firing by `loopId`, keeping it so it can be resumed.

action "resume" — make a paused loop fire again by `loopId`.

action "cancel" — cancel one loop by `loopId`.

action.description: Operation to perform: create, list, pause, resume, or cancel.

prompt.description: Recurring prompt. Required when action is "create".

cron.description: 5-field cron expression in UTC. Pure step cadences are anchored to loop creation.

loopId.description: Loop ID returned by the "list" action. Required when action is "pause", "resume", or "cancel".

runImmediately.description: Also fire once on creation. Defaults to true; only valid for action "create".

tools.description:
List the contents of a directory with optional pattern-based filtering.
Prefer usage of 'Grep' and 'Glob' tools, for more targeted searches.
Supports ignore patterns to exclude unwanted files and directories.

directory_path.description: The absolute path to the directory to list (must be absolute, not relative). Defaults to current working directory if not provided.

ignorePatterns.description: Array of glob patterns to ignore when listing files and directories. Example: ["node_modules/**", "*.log", ".git/**"]

tools.description:
Present a mission plan for user review.

The proposal is the document the user reads to finalize the mission, so write it for a human reader.

The proposal should include:
1. **Plan Overview**: High-level description of what the mission will accomplish
2. **Expected Functionality**: Milestones and features, structured for readability
3. **Architecture**: A section conveying the approved high-level design.
4. **Environment Setup**: Any setup steps needed (dependencies, configuration, etc.)
5. **Infrastructure**: Services, processes, ports, and boundaries (what's allowed/off-limits)
6. **Testing Strategy**: How the mission will be tested, covering which levels apply (unit, component, integration, e2e)
7. **User Testing Strategy**: How manual user testing will work (surfaces to test, tools to use, any setup needed)
8. **Mission Readiness**: The verified dependencies/tools/SDKs the mission will use, and confirmation that the validation path is executable
9. **Non-functional Requirements**

proposal.description: Detailed markdown proposal including: plan overview, environment setup, and user-friendly feature list (not the same as features.json)

workingDirectory.description: Working directory for the mission. Workers will spawn in this directory. Defaults to current cwd if not specified.

tools.description:
Read the contents of a file. A bare read of a long file may open as an outline of its declaration lines, numbered; then pass offset (and limit) to read the lines you need, up to 2400 per call. Short files return whole. Provide line_numbers=true to get lines as `12→text` when you need to cite, page, or check a line (an outline is numbered already); never re-read a file through cat -n, nl or sed for its numbers. Requires absolute file paths.
For image files (JPEG, PNG) up to 5MB, returns the image content you can view and analyze directly; use image_quality="high" (~1MB, 2048px) when details matter. For PDF files up to 3MB, returns the document content.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read (must be absolute, not relative)

offset.description: The line number to start reading from (1-based, defaults to 1)

limit.description: The maximum number of lines to read (defaults to 2400)

line_numbers.description: Prefix each returned line with its line number as `12→text`. Ask for this when you need to cite, page, or check a line, instead of re-reading the file through cat -n, nl or sed. Only applicable when reading text files.

image_quality.description: Image compression quality. "default" uses standard compression (~200KB), "high" uses higher fidelity (~1MB). Only applicable when reading image files.

tools.description: Read one automation by ID from this machine (executionLocation="local") or the cloud (executionLocation="remote"). The result ends with the automation's current prompt in full, between <prompt> tags. Reading a webhook automation also reports its payload filter and its most recent deliveries, which is how you find out why a delivery did not start a run. Reading a Slack automation lists its channels (with ids), channel patterns, keywords, and exclusions in full. A remote read names the chained automations this one starts next and, for any non-CI automation, the automations it is triggered by (the current triggeredByAutomationIds, which an edit replaces in full).

executionLocation.description: Where to read the automation from: "local" for this machine or "remote" for cloud automations.

tools.description: Start a run of a cloud automation right now, by automationId or by automationName, and return without waiting for it to finish. A name is matched exactly (case-insensitive) against the cloud automations ListAutomations shows; if it matches several, the call is refused with their ids so you can ask the user which one they meant. Works for scheduled, webhook, and automation-triggered automations that run on a droid computer, a Factory Environment, or a self-hosted (BYOM) computer that is online; refuses local-only automations and CI- or Slack-triggered ones. When the run ends, the chained automations it starts next (ReadAutomation shows them) start as usual. The run gets no payload or message from you: it sees only its own prompt, and this tool cannot pass it any input. A paused automation still runs. If the automation is already running, the call is skipped rather than failed; do not retry it immediately. Never start the automation that started the current run.

automationId.description: Id of the cloud automation to start (see ListAutomations with executionLocation="remote"). Provide exactly one of automationId or automationName.

automationName.description: Name of the cloud automation to start, matched exactly (case-insensitive) against the automations ListAutomations with executionLocation="remote" shows and resolved to its id at call time. If the name matches multiple automations, ask the user which one to use and retry with its automationId. Provide exactly one of automationId or automationName.

tools.description:
Stage settings, resource, or account changes for the user to review and apply in the desktop chat.

The tool does not apply anything and returns immediately. The user reviews a familiar settings card and explicitly applies each item. You may batch up to 20 requested changes.

Prefer a direct setting operation whenever one matches the request. Use a settings-target operation only when no direct operation covers the requested change. If the user names only a settings page or broad category, use AskUser to identify the exact setting or section before calling this tool. Never guess a specific target and never stage a generic page-opening action. After clarifying an available operation, call this tool with the user's answers. Droid Computer creation is the exception: stage it immediately and let the renderer collect missing details. Do not substitute CLI commands, shell commands, or manual settings instructions for an operation present in the current tool schema.

Use only operation IDs and arguments present in the current tool schema. Never include passwords, API keys, tokens, secret values, or other credentials. Protected values are collected directly from the user by the desktop UI and never enter the transcript. Never claim that a staged change has been applied.

Signal that mission initialization is complete and start the runner.

**This is a blocking call.** The tool call remains open while the mission runner executes workers sequentially. It does NOT return immediately — control stays with the runner until a worker handoff warrants orchestrator attention, the user pauses, or all features complete. Do not expect to perform other actions while this call is in flight.

**Preconditions:**
- {missionDir}/validation-contract.md and validation-state.json must exist and be valid
- {missionDir}/features.json must exist with valid features
- {missionDir}/skills/<skillName>/SKILL.md must exist for each skillName used
- {missionDir}/AGENTS.md must exist with mission guidance
- {missionDir}/services.yaml must exist with commands and service definitions
- {missionDir}/init.sh should exist if environment setup is needed

**Effects:**
- Starts the runner which spawns worker sessions sequentially
- The call blocks until: a worker's handoff has actionable items, the user pauses, or all features complete
- On return, includes workerHandoffs with summaries of all work completed since the last run

message.description: Optional message to log when starting the run

resumeWorkerSessionId.description: Session ID of a previously interrupted worker to resume. If provided, the runner will continue that worker session instead of spawning a new one. Only use this when explicitly resuming after a pause.

restartFeature.description: When true, the in-progress feature will be restarted from scratch with a new worker instead of resuming the paused worker session.

messageToWorker.description: Message delivered to the paused worker when it resumes. A resumed worker picks up mid-session with its existing context, so nothing that happened while it was paused (shared-state updates, new user guidance) reaches it on its own; this message is your channel to the current worker. Pass anything that needs to be communicated to it, and name any files it must reread. Ignored when no paused worker is resumed (fresh workers read shared state at session start).

tools.description:
Launch a subagent for a bounded multi-step task. Use only a `subagent_type` listed below.

Use Task when the work matches an available specialist, can run independently, or requires broad exploration across several files. For a single known file, symbol, or fact, use direct tools. When calling Task, do not issue sibling tool calls for the delegated scope. To run subagents in parallel, issue all of their Task calls in the same assistant message.

Give a self-contained handoff with the goal, context and findings already gathered, constraints, exact remaining work, validation status, and expected output. The report is returned only to you, so relay what matters.

Treat the returned report as your source of record; do not re-read files it covered unless you are about to edit them or the report is incomplete.

Every Task runs in the background: the call returns a task_id immediately and its completed report is delivered to you automatically — do not poll for that delivery with TaskOutput or wait on it with blocking TaskOutput calls (that only burns tokens and delays the delivery); a `block: false` TaskOutput peek at a running task's progress is fine. Once no independent work remains while background Tasks run, end your turn. Their completion will wake you in a new turn with the report; do not poll, sleep, or keep this turn open just to wait. Use `resume` to continue prior context, and pass relevant user-provided image paths through `image_paths`.

Use Task when:
- The work matches a specialized agent.
- Independent work can run in parallel.
- Answering requires broad exploration across several files.
- A long-running task can proceed in the background.

For a known file, symbol, or single fact, use direct tools instead. Do not repeat delegated work.

subagent_type.description: An available agent type from the catalog; do not invent names.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: A self-contained handoff containing the goal, gathered context, constraints, remaining work, validation status, and expected output.

image_paths.description: Optional local image file paths to attach to the subagent. Use this when the original user message included images relevant to the task; pass paths only, never base64 image data.

complexity.description: Optional complexity tier. When the subagent inherits this session's model, caps how hard it reasons (light does not reason at all where the model allows it, heavy reasons most) and never raises it above this session. Also selects the tier model when complexity→model routing is configured in settings. Ignored for custom subagents, which run on their configured model and reasoning effort, or on this session's when they inherit.

resume.description: Task ID (session ID) from a previous invocation to resume with full context preserved

tools.description:
Retrieves output from a running or completed background task.
- Takes a task_id from a directly launched background Task or a Script terminal result's backgroundTasks list
- A background task's completed report is delivered to you automatically; do NOT call TaskOutput in a loop or as a blocking wait for that delivery
- Use block=false to peek at a running task's progress or re-read a finished report
- Use block=true only when you cannot finish the current task without the report
- Returns the task output along with status information
- timeout controls max wait time in ms (default: 30000)

task_id.description: The task ID (session id) to get output from

block.description: Whether to wait for completion (default: true). Completed reports are delivered to you automatically, so prefer block=false progress peeks; reserve blocking for a report you must have before finishing this task.

timeout.description: Max wait time in ms (default: 30000, max: 1200000)

tools.description:
Stops a running background task by its ID.
- Takes a task_id from a directly launched background Task or a Script terminal result's backgroundTasks list
- Sends SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL if the process doesn't stop
- Returns success or failure status

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop

tools.description:
Draft and maintain a structured todo list for the current session so multi-step work and its progress stay visible to the user.

## ALWAYS BATCH THIS CALL
TodoWrite MUST go out in the SAME message as at least one action tool (Read, Grep, Glob, LS, Execute, Edit, Create) whenever a next action exists. Never spend a turn on TodoWrite alone.
- Starting work: emit the list AND your first exploration or action tool together, in one message.
- Advancing work: mark the finished item [completed], mark the next [in_progress], AND issue the next action, all in one message.
A solo TodoWrite produces nothing the user asked for and delays every later step by a full round trip. The only call that may stand alone is the final update, once no work remains.

## Input format
Numbered lines with a status marker; order is determined by line position (max 50 items, 500 chars each):

```
1. [completed] First task that is done
2. [in_progress] Currently working on this
3. [pending] Not started yet
```

## When to use
- The user's task needs 3+ distinct actions/tool calls, the user gives multiple tasks, or the user explicitly asks for todo tracking.
- Skip it for 1-2 step tasks, purely conversational/informational requests, and todos inferred from system context rather than the user's explicit ask.

## Rules
- Keep exactly one [in_progress] item while anything else is [pending]; work on items one at a time.
- Mark [completed] immediately after an item's work is actually done and verified, never while tests fail or the work is partial; if blocked, keep it [in_progress] and add an item for the blocker.
- Write specific, actionable items; preserve user-provided commands and steps verbatim (flags, arguments, order).
- Update the list as new instructions arrive; remove items that have become obsolete or irrelevant instead of leaving them [pending].
- Call TodoWrite in parallel with your first action tools rather than as a separate step; when doing so, mark the started item [in_progress].

Load schemas for deferred tools so they can be called. Two query forms: "select:<name>[,<name>...]" loads the exact names from the "Deferred tools:" system reminder; a keyword query (e.g. "linear issue", or "+slack send" to require "slack" in the tool name) matches words in tool names and auto-loads the best matches. Prefer "select:" when you know the exact name; keywords match names only, never descriptions, so a capability no listed name suggests cannot be found by searching. Never call ToolSearch for a tool that already appears in your current tool list, including one you loaded earlier this session; call it directly instead.

query.description: Query to load deferred tool schemas. Either "select:<name>[,<name>...]" with exact names from the "Deferred tools:" system reminder, or keywords (e.g. "linear issue"; prefix a term with "+" to require it in the tool name, e.g. "+slack send") that match words in tool names and auto-load the best matches.

max_results.description: Maximum number of tools to auto-load for a keyword query (default 5). Ignored for "select:" queries.

tools.description:
Performs a web search to find relevant web pages and documents to the input query. Has options to request full-page text. Do not assume category or search type filters are available. Use this tool ONLY when the query requires finding specific factual information that would benefit from accessing current web content, such as:
      - Recent news, events, or developments
      - Up-to-date statistics, data points, or facts
      - Information about public entities (companies, organizations, people)
      - Specific published content, articles, or references
      - Current trends or technologies
      - API documents for a publicly available API
      - Public github repositories, and other public code resources
    DO NOT use for:
      - Creative generation (writing, poetry, etc.)
      - Mathematical calculations or problem-solving
      - Code generation or debugging unrelated to web resources
      - Finding code files in a repository in factory

    When a query needs a year, take it from the current date in the latest system reminder rather than assuming an older one.

numResults.description: Number of results to return (default: 10). Must be an integer (e.g., 10), not a string. 1-20 allowed. Optional field.

text.description: Whether to include full text content in results. Boolean true/false, not a string.

knowledge.description: Request licensed, current data alongside web results from You.com (for example stock prices, weather, sports, or government spending). Use "core" when the question needs live structured facts rather than web pages.
